query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A sub-eutectic, short-duration tempering treatment will induce the formation of nanoscale ductile interfacial films along the lamellar colony boundaries of the eutectic HEA, thereby reducing dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations. This modification is expected to enhance room-temperature tensile ductility while maintaining or increasing the material’s high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit high strength but limited room-temperature ductility due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted, sub-eutectic, short-duration annealing (tempering) treatment designed to form nanoscale, disordered (or slightly segregated) interfacial layers along the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Treatment performed at temperatures below the eutectic temperature for a short duration, followed by room-temperature tensile testing to assess mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale ductile films at the interlamellar boundaries that act as dislocation sinks and facilitate easier dislocation transmission.
generation.mechanism: By forming ductile interfacial layers, the treatment reduces the buildup of dislocations at the boundaries, alleviating local stress concentrations and suppressing microcrack initiation. This permits a smoother transfer of dislocation motion across the microstructure, enhancing ductility without sacrificing the existing strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in tensile ductility (improved elongation to failure) along with maintained or slightly enhanced yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated material.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA exhibiting high strength but poor room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle failure as a result of dislocation pile-ups at lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.boundary: If the annealing treatment exceeds the optimal parameters, excessive grain boundary coarsening or unwanted phase transformations might occur, potentially compromising the strength. Hence, the benefits are expected only within a defined processing window.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in ductility and the retention or enhancement of strength is uncertain and will depend on the precise tuning of the tempering parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the eutectic HEA: one set remains in the untreated baseline condition while the other undergoes the sub-eutectic, short-duration tempering treatment. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the formation of nanoscale ductile interfacial layers. Then, perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure.
measurements: High-resolution TEM to characterize interfacial structures
Room-temperature tensile tests measuring yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and percentage elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (e.g., less than a 10% improvement in elongation) or if yield and ultimate tensile strengths decrease by more than 5% relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic and refractory HEAs used processing changes (for example, cold rolling and homogenization) to tailor a dual‐phase (lamellar or matrix–precipitate) architecture, which boosted strength but often reduced ductility due to enhanced dislocation pile-up at internal boundaries. Later studies employed thermal treatments—such as short solutionizing/annealing sequences—to partially transform or reconfigure precipitate phases and interfacial structures, thereby opening channels for dislocation transmission and reducing local stress concentrations. However, in systems with intrinsic lamellar colony architectures, the specific control over interfacial structure to alleviate dislocation pile-ups without loss of strength has remained elusive.
decision.unsolved: The challenge is to eliminate or mitigate dislocation pile ups at the lamellar colony (internal) boundaries, which cause local stress concentration and brittle fracture, while not compromising and ideally even enhancing the high strength of the eutectic HEA.
decision.lever: apply a targeted, sub-eutectic, short-duration annealing (tempering) treatment designed to induce nano-scale, structurally disordered (or slightly segregated) interfacial layers along the lamellar colony boundaries
decision.why: This lever directly follows the observed trend in previous work where thermal treatments were leveraged to adjust phase morphologies and precipitate distributions in HEAs. In this case, a carefully optimized tempering treatment would promote the formation of thin, ductile interfacial films that act as dislocation sinks, easing the buildup of dislocations and reducing stress concentrations. This addresses the root cause of brittle behavior by modifying the internal boundaries at the microstructural level—all under room-temperature testing conditions—and builds on supporting prior evidence in similar systems.
